segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision took issue with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter began and set it out for them in order, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: an object coming down, like a great linen sheet being lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right up to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I stared into it and looked closely, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the crawling things, and the birds of the sky.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord! Nothing profane or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But a voice from heaven answered a second time, ‘What God has made clean, you must not call profane.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This happened three times, and then everything was drawn up again into heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And at that very moment three men arrived at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also came with me, and we went into the man’s house.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter;

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: he will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, just as on us at the beginning.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to be able to hinder God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles the turning back that leads to life.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those who had been scattered by the trouble that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who came to Antioch and began speaking to the Greek-speakers as well, proclaiming the good news of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The report about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he encouraged them all to stay with the Lord with resolute hearts,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a sizeable crowd was added to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when he found him he brought him to Antioch. And so for a whole year they met together with the assembly and taught a sizeable crowd, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that there was going to be a great famine over the whole inhabited world. This took place under Claudius.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples decided that each of them, according to their means, would send aid to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

notes.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is one Greek word throughout.

The masculine plural was the ordinary Greek way to address or describe a mixed group of siblings, and here it means the members of the community, women included. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers', and several modern ones have 'brothers and sisters' or 'believers'. In verse 12, where six particular men are meant, 'brothers' is kept.

notes.traditional: they that were of the circumcision / the circumcision party
notes.note: The phrase can simply mean Jewish believers, which at this point is nearly everyone in the Jerusalem community. It can also mean a group within it that held strictly to circumcision. Some translations decide for the second with 'the circumcision party', but the Greek does not settle it and the rendering here leaves it open.

The Greek is blunt: literally 'men having a foreskin'. The charge is not that Peter preached to Gentiles but that he entered their home and shared their table. Many observant Jews avoided this because Gentile food and households were regarded as sources of impurity.

The word ordinarily means 'shared, common'. In Jewish Greek it had become a term for what is ritually ordinary as opposed to holy, and so unfit for a Jew to eat. 'Common' is the traditional rendering, but a modern reader hears it as 'frequent' or 'ordinary'. 'Profane' is used here in its older sense of 'not holy', and the related verb in verse 9 is rendered 'call profane' to keep the echo.

The verb can mean 'to make a distinction' or, mostly in the middle voice, 'to hesitate, to doubt'. The form here is active, which favors 'making no distinction' between Jew and Gentile. Older translations render 'without hesitating', as in the parallel at 10:20. The same verb is used in verse 2 for the critics 'taking issue' with Peter, which may be a deliberate echo.

The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English it centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to 'return' to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct, and 'turning back' is used for it throughout this translation.

Most translations have 'persecution' here, which describes the events of chapter 8 accurately. The Greek word is the general one for distress or affliction, not the specific word for persecution used at 8:1. The plainer rendering keeps the two apart.

Manuscripts are divided between 'Hellenists' (Greek-speakers), the reading translated here, and 'Greeks'. At Acts 6:1 the first word means Greek-speaking Jews. Here the contrast with 'Jews' in verse 19 shows that non-Jews are meant, whichever reading is original. Many translations therefore print 'Greeks'.

The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas 'church' now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs, though it can sound like a single meeting and not a standing community.

The word is formed with a Latin-style ending used for the adherents or partisans of a leader, so it means roughly 'Christ's people'. It appears only three times in the New Testament and is not a name believers use for themselves there. Many scholars think outsiders in Antioch coined it, though this is not certain. The verb can mean either 'were called' or 'took the name'.

The word means the inhabited world, and in common usage often amounted to the Roman empire. Claudius was emperor from AD 41 to 54. Ancient sources mention food shortages in several regions during his reign, including a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s. No single empire-wide famine is recorded, so the phrase is probably a general expression for widespread scarcity.

candidates.reason: The plural for community members recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers', so readers need one policy.
It is rendered variously as tribulation, affliction, persecution, distress and trouble across the New Testament, and needs a default that keeps it distinct from διωγμός.
It recurs in Luke-Acts, Hebrews and Revelation, where 'world', 'inhabited world' and 'empire' are all defensible, and it should be kept distinct from κόσμος.
It covers table service, ministry and material relief (the collection), and translators vary between 'ministry', 'service' and 'relief', so a sense-split decision is needed.

The ritual sense, with the verb κοινόω, recurs in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14 and Hebrews, and is rendered 'common', 'unclean', 'impure', 'defiled' or 'profane'; it must also be kept distinct from ἀκάθαρτος.
